title: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu: Theological Theses (selections)

records.label: Section 1 — Theology names speech about God, and stands to faith as science to understanding
Section 2 — Theology is not required of every person for salvation, yet the church cannot stand without it
Section 3 — The church has never lacked teachers above the faithful people; faith itself requires theological science in the church
Section 4 — Theology is not a science by Aristotle's strict definition, yet it is rightly called science by the evidence of the consequence
Section 5 — Theology is one science by species under divine revelation, and is practical rather than merely speculative
Section 6 — The object of theology is God as the savior of men, not deity considered apart from that respect
Section 7 — Theology's dignity appears from its object — above metaphysics, and wide through creatures, ethics, and history
Section 8 — Theology is also commended by its author — God, not Aristotle or Euclid
Section 9 — Theology surpasses the other sciences in certainty, both in the object and in the habit of faith
Section 10 — Theology's dignity shines most in its end and use — perfect beatitude, not a particular good of this life
Section 11 — Theology is wisely called wisdom: hardest mysteries, and independent of every other science
Section 12 — Theology uses the natural sciences as mistress, judges them, and rightly bears the title Wisdom
Section 13 — Faith is assent to God speaking, moved by divine authority — and not every assent counts as faith
Section 14 — Historical faith names idle assent; temporary faith is shallow joy that collapses under the cross
Section 15 — Miracle-working faith is a special gift; justifying faith is named; Rome confuses it with historical faith

Section 17 — Justifying faith applies the word to practice; it includes the lesser species as the perfect includes the imperfect; assurance of pardon is not its primary act

Section 18 — Faith's object is what God has revealed; Bellarmine misstates it; primary and secondary objects; explicit and implicit faith; revelation measures explicitness; implicit faith is no pretext for ignorance
